headline: Scientists Discover New Cat Species in Bolivia After 100 Years
meta_description: A Bolivian biologist's curiosity about a 'weird cat' led to the discovery of Leopardus tilcayo, the first new feline species identified in over a century.
summary_short: First new cat species in over 100 years identified in Bolivia's Yungas forest. The discovery reshapes our understanding of the entire Leopardus genus.
body:
A persistent Bolivian biologist's refusal to dismiss a curious animal has resulted in the first new feline species to enter the scientific record in over a century. In 2016, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, founder of the Bolivian Felids Research Program and a National Geographic Explorer, received a phone call about a 'weird cat' that a man had brought to a wildlife sanctuary. The animal struck her immediately as unusual: long whiskers, small ears, and distinctive rosettes suggesting it belonged to the genus Leopardus. Though initially thought to be a tigrino—a small cat species common throughout South America—Nogales-Ascarrunz noticed striking differences three years later while preparing a regional cat species guide. This observation prompted a six-year investigation into genomic analysis that ultimately proved she had discovered something entirely new. Published in Cell, the research describes Leopardus tilcayo, named after the indigenous Bolivian term for the animal. The tilcayo diverged from its nearest relative approximately 1.4 million years ago, giving it evolutionary standing comparable to the divergence between modern lions and extinct cave lions.

What makes the discovery particularly remarkable is how little we actually know about the creature. Scientists have confirmed only that it inhabits the Yungas forest ecosystem on the eastern slopes of the Bolivian Andes. Its diet, reproduction, social behavior, and other ecological details remain complete mysteries waiting to be uncovered.

The tilcayo's identification has rippled far beyond a single species discovery. Working alongside geneticist Eduardo Eizirik at Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil, Nogales-Ascarrunz's research has fundamentally reshaped understanding of the entire Leopardus genus. What was once believed to be a single species has revealed itself as a complex collection of distinct species—expanding from eight recognized species in 2020 to potentially more today. The discovery reminds us that exploration isn't finished; the world remains far more complex and unknown than we typically assume.
quick_facts: First new feline species identified since 1923
Found in Bolivia's Yungas forest ecosystem, eastern Andes slopes
Named Leopardus tilcayo, using indigenous Bolivian community's traditional name
Diverged from nearest relative approximately 1.4 million years ago
Discovery reshapes scientific understanding of entire Leopardus genus
